paragraphs.heading: Forgetting how common things are
paragraphs.text: The base rate fallacy is the error of ignoring the base rate, meaning how common something is in general, and focusing only on details about one specific case. It also goes by the names base rate neglect and base rate bias. It is a particular form of a broader error known as extension neglect.

paragraphs.heading: In the courtroom
paragraphs.text: When the mistake is made with statistical test results in a legal case, such as DNA tests, it is called the prosecutor's fallacy or the defense attorney's fallacy. William C. Thompson and Edward Schumann introduced these terms in 1987. Some have argued that their idea of the prosecutor's fallacy covers further wrong conclusions about guilt that are not really errors about base rates or Bayes's theorem.

paragraphs.heading: Too many false alarms
paragraphs.text: One example is the false positive paradox, where a test produces more false positives than true positives. Picture a face-recognition camera that spots wanted criminals with 99% accuracy but scans 10,000 people a day. Because innocent people vastly outnumber criminals, its list of suspects will likely hold far more innocents than criminals. How often a test comes back positive depends on the people being tested as well as on how accurate the test is.

paragraphs.heading: Why rarity matters
paragraphs.text: When a condition is rarer than the test's false positive rate, even a test that seldom errs on any single person gives more false positives than true ones overall. A tiny slice of the huge healthy group simply outnumbers a large slice of the small sick group. In one illustration, a person in population A who tests positive can be over 93% confident the result is right. In population B, only 20 of the 69 positives were truly infected, about 29%, for a test that seems "95% accurate". Someone used to group A may find it a paradox that in group B a positive result is now usually false.

paragraphs.heading: The breathalyzer test
paragraphs.text: Suppose police breathalyzers wrongly show drunkenness for 5% of sober drivers but never miss a drunk one, and one driver in a thousand is drunk. Officers stop a driver at random, and the test says drunk. Many people would put the chance that the driver is drunk at 95%, but the right answer is about 2%. Among the 1 + 49.95 = 50.95 positive results, only 1 belongs to a drunk driver, giving 1/50.95 ≈ 1.9627%. This holds only if the driver really was stopped at random, not for driving badly.

paragraphs.heading: The alarm bell
paragraphs.text: Picture a city of 1 million people with 100 terrorists, so the base rate is 0.0001. A camera rings a bell for 99% of terrorists it scans and also for 1% of everyone else. If someone sets off the bell, a person making the base rate fallacy would say there is a 99% chance they are a terrorist. In fact the chance is close to 1%. The mistake mixes up two different rates: how often the bell stays silent for a terrorist, and how often a ringing bell points at an innocent person.
